title: Benchmarking knowledge transfer methods in de novo materials discovery
experiments_summary: Three generative models — REINVENT (GRU-based RNN trained on ChEMBL 25), MolMIM (VAE+MIM trained on ZINC-15), and Mol-AIR (LSTM-based RL framework trained on ChEMBL 29) — were benchmarked across 30 distinct configurations on two molecular representations of Covalent Triazine Frameworks (CTFs): substrates and lattice nodes. Configurations varied by training strategy (pre-training only, fine-tuning only, reinforcement learning, combinations thereof, and with/without seed molecules), using either ZINC-15 or ChEMBL 35 as pre-training data and a manually curated set of 103 CTFs (substrates and lattice nodes encoded as SMILES) for fine-tuning. Pre-training was performed on large public databases; fine-tuning used the curated CTF dataset. Reinforcement learning for REINVENT and Mol-AIR used an expert-defined reward function incorporating five material-specific criteria: (1) presence of chemical patterns enabling cyclization (binary, via RDKit/SMARTS), (2) symmetry assessed via Continuous Symmetry Measure (CSM) for C2/C3/C4 groups mapped to a 0–1 score with exponential decay outside an optimal range of 0–5, (3) flatness evaluated by fitting a plane to 3D molecular conformations via linear regression and computing RMSE with a threshold of 6.0, (4) conjugation determined by checking electron-transfer paths between nitrogen atoms, and (5) steric hindrance criteria. Policy collapse mitigation strategies were implemented as described in appendices. All training was conducted on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with a 72-hour time budget per configuration. Evaluation employed ten independent sampling repetitions per configuration; REINVENT and Mol-AIR generated 10,000 molecules per repetition while MolMIM sampled 100 molecules per training instance. Six metrics were computed: validity, uniqueness, internal diversity (Tanimoto-based), Fréchet ChemNet Distance (FCD), novelty, and percentage of molecules passing the expert-defined filters.
